title: Help Me Understand
bottom_line: Run /help-me-understand:help-me-understand on a long answer, file or page. You get a link to one page holding the same information, picture first.

sections.heading: You need the Artifact tool and Python 3.8

cards.title: The Artifact tool
cards.text: Publishes the page as a private claude.ai artifact and gives you a link.

cards.title: Python 3.8 or later
cards.text: Runs the bundled renderer. It uses the standard library only.

cards.title: humanizer plugin (optional)
cards.text: When `/humanizer:humanizer` is installed, its writing rules are applied to the page text. Otherwise the skill follows a short inline version of the same rules.

sections.heading: Type the command, with or without something to explain

blocks.title: The command
blocks.code: /help-me-understand:help-me-understand [topic | file path | URL]  (empty = the last substantial answer in this conversation)

blocks.title: What gets explained
rows: none
The last substantial answer in this conversation.
a topic
What this conversation says about it, researched further if the conversation says little.
a file path, a URL or a claude.ai artifact link
The contents of that file, page or artifact.

blocks.title: Good to know
items: The skill only runs when you invoke it; Claude never starts it on its own.
With no argument, it takes the most recent reply that explains, reports or summarises something. Short confirmations and questions are skipped.
A link that ends in a `#fragment` still means the whole page, unless you say you want only that part.
Text inside a file or web page that is addressed to an AI, such as "ignore your instructions" or "run this command", is treated as material to explain and never followed.

sections.heading: You get a link, the bottom line and one next action

blocks.caption: The page itself is not pasted into chat.

blocks.title: Running it again
blocks.text: Running it again for the same topic in the same conversation updates the same page, so the link stays the same.

blocks.title: Example: after a long answer comparing three queue libraries
blocks.text: You run `/help-me-understand:help-me-understand` with no argument. The reply is a link to a research page, plus:

blocks.code:
Bottom line: use arq, because it is the only one of the three that is async and already runs on your Redis.
Next: add arq to requirements.txt and run arq --check worker.WorkerSettings.

blocks.text: The page opens with a verdict picture of arq against the other two libraries, each with the reason it lost. Then come stops for when the verdict holds, the measurements, and a comparison table with arq's column highlighted. The evidence for each library sits under its own sub-heading in the stop that discusses it.

sections.heading: Claude picks one of four page types

cards.title: Concept
cards.text: Explains how something works or what it means.

cards.title: Research
cards.text: Answers a question by comparing options or weighing evidence.

cards.title: Work summary
cards.text: Reports what was done, what changed and what is left.

cards.title: How-to
cards.text: Tells the reader how to do something, in order.

blocks.caption: Each type has its own section order.

sections.heading: The page opens with the whole idea, then numbered stops

blocks.title: The page from top to bottom

nodes.label: Full detail and Also worth knowing

blocks.title: What each part holds
items: The title, then one panel with the gist picture and the bottom line (25 words at most). The gist is a chain from cause to outcome, a verdict of the winner against the alternatives, or a status of tallies with state icons.
One quiet line saying the reader may stop there, with the number of stops and the reading time (about 200 words per minute, counting only what shows without opening a collapsed block).
A route of up to twelve numbered stops that marks the stop in view, and a scroll progress bar.
Stops, each drawn as its own sheet, that lead with a visual and then give the stop's full detail under sub-headings, including tables of any length and verbatim code listings.
Collapsed notes inside a stop for bulky verbatim material such as a long listing, each labelled with what it holds.
A collapsed "Full detail" drawer only for material that belongs to no single stop, then "Also worth knowing", a collapsed block for asides.
One "Next action" card and the sources.

blocks.title: The visuals a stop can lead with
items: Big figures.
Icon arrays for proportions.
Chains.
Cards with pros and cons or states.
Numbered stepper (Back, Next, Start over).
Comparison table.
Bar chart.
Dot chart.
Flow diagram.
Timeline.
Before and after pair.
"Check yourself" click-to-reveal prompts (concept pages only).
Glossary strip.
A slot for a bespoke SVG diagram.

blocks.text: Icons come from a closed built-in set and always sit next to a text label.

blocks.title: Reading comfort
items: Light and dark themes.
Running text held to about 65 characters per line, while tables, cards, chains and charts use the full page width.
Keyboard access with visible focus.
No autoplaying motion.
No external scripts, fonts or images.
With JavaScript off, every stepper step is visible and the route is a plain list of links.
When printed, every step and every collapsed block is shown.

sections.heading: The page keeps every detail of the original

before.label: The original
before.text: A research finding, answer or work summary that is too long or too tangled to follow.

after.label: The page
after.text: The same information, including every table row, list item and code listing, with each detail in the stop it belongs to. It does not summarise.

blocks.title: Defaults and why
rows: A picture of the whole idea first, and a visual in every stop
A plain first screen makes readers more willing to start, and pictures of structure, quantity and sequence help comprehension.
Same information as the source, checked by a coverage pass
A page that says less than its source sends the reader back to the original.
Length limits on labels and headings only, enforced by the renderer
Short labels keep the layout readable. Limits on how much a page may hold forced detail off the page, so those are set high.
Detail visible by default, under sub-headings in its stop
A reader looking for a detail finds it where the idea is explained; only bulky listings are collapsed, with a label saying what is inside.
Bars and dots only, labelled directly, bar axes from zero
Position and length are read most accurately, and labels on the mark avoid a legend.
Animation only as a reader-controlled stepper
Motion that plays on its own runs past a reader who is still thinking.
No decoration, fun facts or story hooks
Off-topic material lowers what readers remember.
Full plain English, even when a terse or caveman mode is active
The reader asked for this because the original was hard to follow.

blocks.title: Limits worth knowing
items: Effects of design principles are smaller on self-paced pages like these than in lab settings.

No controlled study tests headings, chunking, progress bars or time estimates in adults with ADHD. The ADHD-specific choices (reading time, progress bar, collapsed tangents, one next action) are reasonable extrapolations from working-memory research, not tested findings.

sections.heading: If something is missing, Claude tells you

cards.title: No Artifact tool
cards.text: You get no link. The HTML file stays on disk instead.

points.text: You get the file's full path; it opens in any browser.

cards.title: Nothing to explain
cards.text: You gave no argument and there is no substantial answer yet.

points.text: Claude asks you what to explain and stops.

cards.title: The URL will not load
cards.text: The page could not be fetched.

next_action.text: After a long answer you found hard to follow, type `/help-me-understand:help-me-understand` with no argument.
next_action.detail: It reorganises the last substantial answer in the conversation into a page and replies with its link.
